claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: WTb inhibited HDV binding to PTHs with efficiency comparable to Myr-47/WT that is comprised of all natural amino acids.
claims.source: WTb inhibited HDV binding to PTHs with efficiency comparable to Myr-47/WT that is comprised of all natural amino acids (Figure 1A,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1A and 1C.

claims.claim: A peptide Myr-47/N9Kb (or N9Kb hereafter) similar to WTb but with an additional mutation at the ninth residue (N9K) did not block HDV binding to PTHs.
claims.source: A peptide Myr-47/N9Kb (or N9Kb hereafter) similar to WTb but with an additional mutation at the ninth residue (N9K) did not block HDV binding to PTHs (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: WTb but not N9Kb inhibited viral infection of HBV and HDV on PTHs.
claims.source: WTb but not N9Kb inhibited viral infection of HBV and HDV on PTHs (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Western blotting using 2D3 as a probe revealed several bands including a major smeared band with apparent molecular weight of ∼65 kDa in the WTb but not N9Kb cross-linked sample.
claims.source: Western blotting using 2D3 as a probe revealed several bands including a major smeared band with apparent molecular weight of ∼65 kDa in the WTb but not N9Kb cross-linked sample.
claims.evidence: This claim describes experimental observations from Western blotting.

claims.claim: The 65-kDa band shifted to ∼43 kDa upon treatment with the deglycosylation enzyme PNGase F.
claims.source: The 65-kDa band shifted to ∼43 kDa upon treatment with the deglycosylation enzyme PNGase F (Figure 2A, left), indicating that it is highly N-glycosylated.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The WTb cross-linked protein apparently contained no intermolecular disulfide bonds as it migrated similarly under both nonreducing and reducing conditions.
claims.source: The WTb cross-linked protein apparently contained no intermolecular disulfide bonds as it migrated similarly under both nonreducing and reducing conditions (Figure 2A, right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The non-photoreactive Myr-47/WT peptide but not its N9K mutant peptide effectively competed with WTb for cross-linking to the 65-kDa band.
claims.source: The non-photoreactive Myr-47/WT peptide but not its N9K mutant peptide effectively competed with WTb for cross-linking to the 65-kDa band (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The cross-linked protein from PTHs decreased in abundance rapidly over time during culture.
claims.source: The cross-linked protein from PTHs decreased in abundance rapidly over time during culture (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Bands with slightly smaller molecular weights than those seen in the PTH cells were also observed in PHHs.
claims.source: Bands with slightly smaller molecular weights than those seen in the PTH cells were also observed in PHHs (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Two different tryptic peptide fragments, which were identified from both the ∼65-kDa and ∼43-kDa bands, matched to a protein homolog of human NTCP.
claims.source: Two different tryptic peptide fragments, which were identified from both the ∼65-kDa and ∼43-kDa bands (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), matched to a protein homolog of human NTCP.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Tupaia NTCP (tsNTCP) shares 83.9% protein sequence identity with its human counterpart and has an insertion of 30 aa near its C-terminus.
claims.source: Tupaia NTCP (tsNTCP) shares 83.9% protein sequence identity with its human counterpart and has an insertion of 30 aa near its C-terminus (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Both human NTCP (hNTCP) and tsNTCP could be efficiently cross-linked by WTb but not N9Kb when expressed in 293T cells.
claims.source: Both human NTCP (hNTCP) and tsNTCP could be efficiently cross-linked by WTb but not N9Kb when expressed in 293T cells as shown by Western blotting with the anti-WTb antibody 2D3 as well as an anti-C9 antibody recognizing the C-terminal C9 tag of the recombinant hNTCP and tsNTCP proteins (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: WTb but not the control N9Kb peptide bound to 293T cells expressing a green fluorescent protein (GFP)-tagged tsNTCP (tsNTCP-EGFP) and co-localized with tsNTCP-EGFP on the cell surface.
claims.source: WTb but not the control N9Kb peptide bound to 293T cells expressing a green fluorescent protein (GFP)-tagged tsNTCP (tsNTCP-EGFP) and co-localized with tsNTCP-EGFP on the cell surface. This binding was readily competed off by the free Myr-47/WT peptide (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: A native pre-S1 peptide specifically recognized the human hepatocellular carcinoma Huh-7 cell line transfected with hNTCP.
claims.source: Moreover, a native pre-S1 peptide specifically recognized the human hepatocellular carcinoma Huh-7 cell line transfected with hNTCP (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Huh-7 cells transfected with either tsNTCP or hNTCPs had markedly increased HDV binding to the cells.
claims.source: Consistently, Huh-7 cells transfected with either tsNTCP or hNTCPs had markedly increased HDV binding to the cells.
claims.evidence: This claim describes experimental observations from HDV binding assays.

claims.claim: The Myr-47/WT peptide readily competed with binding of the wild-type HDV, whereas a noninfectious mutant HDV virus bearing a single N9K mutation in the pre-S1 domain of its L envelope protein failed to bind either hNTCP- or tsNTCP-expressing Huh-7 cells.
claims.source: The Myr-47/WT peptide readily competed with binding of the wild-type HDV, whereas a noninfectious mutant HDV virus bearing a single N9K mutation in the pre-S1 domain of its L envelope protein failed to bind either hNTCP- or tsNTCP-expressing Huh-7 cells (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: When tsNTCP mRNA level was reduced to ∼30% in tsNTCP siRNA-transfected cells, total HDV RNA copies were markedly reduced in these cells comparing to those transfected with control siRNA.
claims.source: When tsNTCP mRNA level was reduced to ∼30% in tsNTCP siRNA-transfected cells (Figure 4A, upper-left), total HDV RNA copies were markedly reduced in these cells comparing to those transfected with control siRNA.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Both HDV genomic and antigenomic RNA copies were greatly reduced in cells transfected with tsNTCP-specific siRNA but not the control siRNA.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 4A (upper-middle panel), both HDV genomic and antigenomic RNA copies were greatly reduced in cells transfected with tsNTCP-specific siRNA but not the control siRNA, indicating that tsNTCP is required for de novo HDV infection.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Lenti-VSV-G virus infection, for which viral entry is mediated by glycoprotein protein G of VSV, was not affected in the tsNTCP- and siRNA-transfected cells.
claims.source: By contrast, lenti-VSV-G virus infection, for which viral entry is mediated by glycoprotein protein G of VSV, was not affected in the tsNTCP- and siRNA-transfected cells (Figure 4A, upper-right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Both HBsAg and HBeAg levels were markedly reduced by transfection of tsNTCP-specific but not a control siRNA at all three time points tested.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 4A (lower-left), both HBsAg and HBeAg levels were markedly reduced by transfection of tsNTCP-specific but not a control siRNA at all three time points tested, demonstrating that tsNTCP expression is required for bona fide HBV infection.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: NTCP knockdown did not affect AAV8-HBV infection in PTHs.
claims.source: NTCP knockdown did not affect AAV8-HBV infection in PTHs, as shown by the kinetics of HBeAg (Figure 4A, lower-right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The NTCP mRNA level was low in HepaRG cells before induction when examined on days 5 and 10 after initial plating, but increased dramatically when the cells differentiated after induction.
claims.source: The NTCP mRNA level was low in HepaRG cells before induction when examined on days 5 and 10 after initial plating, but increased dramatically when the cells differentiated after induction (Figure 4B, upper-left).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: About 70% HDV infection was reduced by hNTCP knockdown as indicated by decreased levels of HDV viral RNAs.
claims.source: About 70% HDV infection was reduced by hNTCP knockdown as indicated by decreased levels of HDV viral RNAs (Figure 4B, upper-right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: HBV infection was inhibited by hNTCP knockdown in HepaRG cells as indicated by significantly reduced HBeAg at multiple time points, as well as viral RNAs including the 3.5 kb RNA for HBV pre-C and pregenome RNA (pgRNA) and HBV total RNA quantified at the end of the experiment.
claims.source: Similarly, HBV infection was also inhibited as indicated by significantly reduced HBeAg at multiple time points (Figure 4B, lower-left), as well as viral RNAs including the 3.5 kb RNA for HBV pre-C and pregenome RNA (pgRNA) and HBV total RNA (Figure 4B, lower-right) quantified at the end of the experiment.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Knockdown of hNTCP significantly reduced HBV infection in PHHs, which was correlated with the NTCP mRNA knockdown efficiency.
claims.source: Consistently, knockdown of hNTCP significantly reduced HBV infection, which was correlated with the NTCP mRNA knockdown efficiency. Both viral antigens and viral RNAs were decreased in cells transfected with hNTCP-specific siRNAs but not with the control siRNA (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: NTCP mRNA expression is low in human hepatocarcinoma cell lines that are not susceptible to HBV or HDV infection.
claims.source: NTCP mRNA expression is low in human hepatocarcinoma cell lines that are not susceptible to HBV or HDV infection.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about NTCP expression in cell lines, presented as an observation.

claims.claim: The levels of NTCP mRNA in Huh-7 and HepG2 cells were about 10,000 times lower than that in primary human and Tupaia hepatocytes.
claims.source: The levels of NTCP mRNA in Huh-7 and HepG2 cells were about 10,000 times lower than that in primary human and Tupaia hepatocytes (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Human NTCP-transfected Huh-7 cells supported HDV infection with an efficiency comparable to that of PTHs; nearly 10% of cells were infected as shown by staining of the HDV delta antigen that mainly locates in cell nuclei, whereas Huh-7 cells transfected with a vector plasmid allowed no HDV infection.
claims.source: Human NTCP-transfected Huh-7 cells supported HDV infection with an efficiency comparable to that of PTHs; nearly 10% of cells were infected as shown by staining of the HDV delta antigen that mainly locates in cell nuclei, whereas Huh-7 cells transfected with a vector plasmid allowed no HDV infection (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The infection of HDV in hNTCP-transfected Huh-7 cells could be blocked by known HBV entry inhibitors, such as pre-S1 lipopeptide and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG).
claims.source: Moreover, the infection could be blocked by known HBV entry inhibitors, such as pre-S1 lipopeptide and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG), demonstrating a genuine infection of HDV mediated by HBV envelope proteins on these cells (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: HDV RNAs, including antigenomic RNA that is only produced during HDV replication, rapidly increased over time in the infected hNTCP-transfected Huh-7 cells.
claims.source: HDV RNAs, including antigenomic RNA that is only produced during HDV replication, rapidly increased over time in the infected cells (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The infection efficiency of HDV in hNTCP-transfected Huh-7 cells correlated with both the inoculation dose of HDV and the expression level of hNTCP.
claims.source: Moreover, the infection efficiency correlated with both the inoculation dose of HDV (Figure 5E) and the expression level of hNTCP (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claims.claim: HepG2 cells transiently transfected with either tsNTCP- or hNTCP-supported HBV infection as evidenced by continuous secretion of HBeAg over time and accumulation of HBV replicative intermediate viral RNAs in the infected cells.
claims.source: HepG2 cells transiently transfected with either tsNTCP- or hNTCP-supported HBV infection as evidenced by continuous secretion of HBeAg over time and accumulation of HBV replicative intermediate viral RNAs in the infected cells. The entry inhibitor Myr-59 blocked the infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: About 5–10% of stable HepG2-hNTCP cells were infected with HBV as revealed by intracellular staining of HBsAg, whereas there was no HBV infection in the parental HepG2 cells.
claims.source: More efficient HBV infection was achieved on stable HepG2-hNTCP cells with about 5–10% of the cells being infected as revealed by intracellular staining of HBsAg, whereas there was no HBV infection in the parental HepG2 cells (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: HBV entry inhibitors, in particular the Myr-59 peptide and 17B9, efficiently inhibited the infection of HepG2-hNTCP cells.
claims.source: HBV entry inhibitors, in particular the Myr-59 peptide and 17B9, efficiently inhibited the infection (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The infection efficiency of HBV in HepG2-hNTCP cells as evidenced by HBV total and 3.5 kb RNA levels correlated with the inoculation dose.
claims.source: The infection efficiency as evidenced by HBV total and 3.5 kb RNA levels correlated with the inoculation dose.
claims.evidence: This claim describes experimental observations from HBV infection assays.

claims.claim: The formation of HBV covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA), which is a replicative intermediate and transcriptional template for production of viral RNAs, was confirmed by Southern blot analysis in HepG2-hNTCP cells.
claims.source: Moreover, the formation of HBV covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA), which is a replicative intermediate and transcriptional template for production of viral RNAs, was confirmed by Southern blot analysis (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: HBV cccDNA became detectable at 24 hr post-infection in HepG2-hNTCP cells, markedly increased at day 3 post-infection and maintained a relatively stable level for the rest of the time points examined.
claims.source: The cccDNA became detectable at 24 hr post-infection. It markedly increased at day 3 post-infection and maintained a relatively stable level for the rest of the time points examined, whereas the formation of HBV cccDNA was completely abolished if entry inhibitor Myr-59 was included with the initial virus inoculation (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: HBV RNA levels of the 3.5 kb transcript and the total HBV transcripts in the infected HepG2-hNTCP cells gradually increased during first several days of infection and reached a steady level after day 5.
claims.source: Consistently, HBV RNA levels of the 3.5 kb transcript and the total HBV transcripts in the infected HepG2-hNTCP cells gradually increased during first several days of infection and reached a steady level after day 5 (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Crab-eating monkey (Macaca fascicularis) NTCP (mkNTCP) shares high protein sequence identity with hNTCP (96.3%).
claims.source: Crab-eating monkey (Macaca fascicularis) NTCP (mkNTCP) shares high protein sequence identity with hNTCP (96.3%) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: mkNTCP neither supports HDV infection nor pre-S1 peptide (Myr-59) binding.
claims.source: However, mkNTCP neither supports HDV infection nor pre-S1 peptide (Myr-59) binding (Figure 7A), consistent with the known narrow species specificity of the virus.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Alteration of five residues of hNTCP between aa 157–165 and its monkey counterpart (from KGIVISLVL to GRIILSLVP) completely abolished Myr-59 binding and the ability to support HDV infection.
claims.source: Whereas most mutations did not significantly interfere with Myr-59 binding or HDV infection, alteration of five residues of hNTCP between aa 157–165 and its monkey counterpart (from KGIVISLVL to GRIILSLVP, distinct residues are underlined) completely abolished Myr-59 binding and the ability to support HDV infection.
claims.evidence: This claim describes experimental observations from mutagenesis studies.

claims.claim: Replacing the motif of aa 167–156 in mkNTCP with the corresponding human residues converted mkNTCP to an efficient receptor for HDV infection.
claims.source: Remarkably, replacing the motif of aa 167–156 in mkNTCP with the corresponding human residues converted mkNTCP to an efficient receptor for HDV infection (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: HBV infection was abolished on HepG2 cells expressing hNTCP carrying monkey-like mutations, GRIILSLVP, while mkNTCP-bearing human residues KGIVISLVL within the motif of aa 157–165 largely restored HBV infection.
claims.source: Similar to HDV, HBV infection was also abolished on HepG2 cells expressing hNTCP carrying monkey-like mutations, GRIILSLVP, while mkNTCP-bearing human residues KGIVISLVL within the motif of aa 157–165 largely restored HBV infection (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Residues between 157 and 165 of NTCP are crucial for binding to the receptor-binding region of the pre-S1 domain of the L protein of HBV, and critically contribute to NTCP-mediated HBV and HDV infections.
claims.source: These data show that residues between 157 and 165 of NTCP are crucial for binding to the receptor-binding region of the pre-S1 domain of the L protein of HBV, and critically contribute to NTCP-mediated HBV and HDV infections.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the mutagenesis experiments described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: NTCP is a functional receptor for both HBV and HDV.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that NTCP is a functional receptor for HBV and HDV.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: An N-terminal myristoylated peptide corresponding to amino acids (aa) 2–48 of the pre-S1 domain of the L protein has been shown to effectively block both HBV and HDV infections of hepatocytes through engaging an unknown cellular component, most likely a viral receptor.
claims.source: An N-terminal myristoylated peptide corresponding to amino acids (aa) 2–48 of the pre-S1 domain of the L protein has been shown to effectively block both HBV and HDV infections of hepatocytes through engaging an unknown cellular component, most likely a viral receptor (Barrera et al., 2005; Glebe et al., 2005; Gripon et al., 2005; Engelke et al., 2006; Schulze et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: NTCP (Slc10a1) is the founding member of the SLC10 family of solute carrier proteins.
claims.source: NTCP (Slc10a1) is the founding member of the SLC10 family of solute carrier proteins.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about NTCP classification, presented as established knowledge.

claims.claim: NTCP is a hepatic Na+ bile acid symporter and is responsible for cotransportation of sodium and bile acids across cellular membranes to maintain the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids.
claims.source: It is a hepatic Na+ bile acid symporter and is responsible for cotransportation of sodium and bile acids across cellular membranes to maintain the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids (Hagenbuch and Meier, 1994; Stieger, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hagenbuch and Meier, 1994 and Stieger, 2011.

claims.claim: NTCP is a multiple transmembrane glycoprotein presumed to span the cellular membrane up to 10 times with small extracellular loops.
claims.source: NTCP is a multiple transmembrane glycoprotein presumed to span the cellular membrane up to 10 times with small extracellular loops (Mareninova et al., 2005; Hu et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mareninova et al., 2005 and Hu et al., 2011.

claims.claim: NTCP is mainly expressed in the liver.
claims.source: It is mainly expressed in the liver (Stieger, 2011), consistent with the liver tropism of HBV and HDV.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stieger, 2011.

claims.claim: NTCP localizes to the sinusoidal (basolateral) plasma membrane of hepatocytes.
claims.source: NTCP localizes to the sinusoidal (basolateral) plasma membrane of hepatocytes (Stieger et al., 1994), a location that fits well with its receptor role for blood-borne HBV and HDV.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stieger et al., 1994.

claims.claim: HBV first attaches to hepatocytes mainly through heparan sulfate.
claims.source: Whereas HBV first attaches to hepatocytes mainly through heparan sulfate (Schulze et al., 2007; Leistner et al., 2008), our data demonstrate that the interaction between NTCP and L protein of HBV is highly specific, and NTCP is crucial for productive viral entry of hepatocytes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schulze et al., 2007 and Leistner et al., 2008.

claims.claim: NTCP expression rapidly decreased over time in cultured PTHs after isolation.
claims.source: Consistent with previous reports on primary cultures of rat hepatocytes (Liang et al., 1993; Rippin et al., 2001), NTCP expression rapidly decreased over time in cultured PTHs after isolation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liang et al., 1993 and Rippin et al., 2001, and by experimental data in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Primary hepatocytes typically remain susceptible to HBV infections in vitro for only a few days after isolation from liver tissues.
claims.source: This may at least partially explain the observations that primary hepatocytes typically remain susceptible to HBV infections in vitro for only a few days after isolation from liver tissues (Gripon et al., 1988; Seeger et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gripon et al., 1988 and Seeger et al., 2007.

claims.claim: NTCP expression is low and inversely correlated with the degree of dedifferentiation of cancer cells in human hepatocellular carcinoma.
claims.source: NTCP expression is low and inversely correlated with the degree of dedifferentiation of cancer cells in human hepatocellular carcinoma (Kullak-Ublick et al., 1997; Zollner et al., 2005) and the severity of HBV-related liver cirrhosis (Lee and Kim, 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kullak-Ublick et al., 1997 and Zollner et al., 2005.

claims.claim: NTCP expression is inversely correlated with the severity of HBV-related liver cirrhosis.
claims.source: NTCP expression is low and inversely correlated with the degree of dedifferentiation of cancer cells in human hepatocellular carcinoma (Kullak-Ublick et al., 1997; Zollner et al., 2005) and the severity of HBV-related liver cirrhosis (Lee and Kim, 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee and Kim, 2007.

claims.claim: About 10% HepG2-NTCP cells were infected with HBV at multiplicities of genome equivalents (mge) of 100, which is comparable to the efficiency of HBV infection of PHHs.
claims.source: As shown by intracellular staining of HBV core antigen (HBcAg) on day 8 post-infection, about 10% HepG2-NTCP cells were infected at multiplicities of genome equivalents (mge) of 100, which is comparable to the efficiency of HBV infection of PHHs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The level of secreted HBeAg from HepG2-NTCP appeared to be higher than that in PHHs from two donors, whereas the levels of viral RNAs per nanogram of total cell RNA in both infected cell types are comparable.
claims.source: The level of secreted HBeAg from HepG2-NTCP appeared to be higher than that in PHHs from two donors, whereas the levels of viral RNAs per nanogram of total cell RNA in both infected cell types are comparable (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Efficient HBV infection of PHHs or HepaRG cells in vitro normally requires high dose of virus inoculums, and only limited progeny viruses are produced after infection.
claims.source: Efficient HBV infection of PHHs or HepaRG cells in vitro normally requires high dose of virus inoculums, and only limited progeny viruses are produced after infection (Gripon et al., 1988; Gripon et al., 2002; Boehm et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gripon et al., 1988; Gripon et al., 2002; and Boehm et al., 2005.

claims.claim: The levels of viral DNA in the media resulted from the ongoing infection during days 4–13 post-infection were low (equivalent to ∼1% of input viral DNA copies) despite significant amount of HBeAg secretion during this period in HepG2-NTCP cells.
claims.source: The levels of viral DNA in the media resulted from the ongoing infection during days 4–13 post-infection were low (equivalent to ∼1% of input viral DNA copies) despite significant amount of HBeAg secretion during this period.
claims.evidence: This claim describes experimental observations from viral DNA quantification assays.

claims.claim: Only low levels of viral DNA were detected in the medium from HBV-infected PHHs.
claims.source: Similarly, only low levels of viral DNA were detected in the medium from HBV-infected PHHs (Figure 6—figure supplement 4, right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Very low number of intracellular HBV total RNA copies were detected in PHHs on day 13 post-infection with culture medium collected from infected HepG2-NTCP cells.
claims.source: In line with the low HBV viral DNA level in the medium inoculum, very low number of intracellular HBV total RNA copies were detected in PHHs on day 13 post-infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 5), indicating that only very limited HBV infection might have occurred, which may be attributed to the low multiplicity of infection.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Treeshrews (Tupaia belangeri) are the only species susceptible to human HBV infection other than humans and chimpanzees.
claims.source: Primary hepatocytes isolated from treeshrews (Tupaia belangeri), the only species susceptible to human HBV infection other than humans and chimpanzees (Su et al., 1987; Walter et al., 1996; Glebe et al., 2003), were used as target cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Su et al., 1987; Walter et al., 1996; and Glebe et al., 2003.

claims.claim: HepaRG is the only cell line known to date to be susceptible to HBV and HDV infections upon differentiation into a mixture of hepatocyte-like and biliary-like cells.
claims.source: Human hepatoma cell line HepaRG is the only cell line known to date to be susceptible to HBV and HDV infections upon differentiation into a mixture of hepatocyte-like and biliary-like cells (Gripon et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gripon et al., 2002.

claims.claim: HepaRG differentiation requires a lengthy cell culture procedure, including maintaining undifferentiated cells for 2 weeks before induction, followed by induction with corticoids and DMSO for another 2–4 weeks.
claims.source: HepaRG differentiation requires a lengthy cell culture procedure, including maintaining undifferentiated cells for 2 weeks before induction, followed by induction with corticoids and DMSO for another 2–4 weeks (Gripon et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gripon et al., 2002.

claims.claim: HDV is enveloped by HBV envelope proteins and can only infect target cells in a single round in the absence of HBV.
claims.source: As HDV is enveloped by HBV envelope proteins and can only infect target cells in a single round in the absence of HBV, these data support that tsNTCP functions at entry level for viral infection mediated by HBV envelope proteins.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about HDV biology, presented as established knowledge.

claims.claim: The HDV antigenome is a circular replication intermediate that is complementary to the genome and is not present in the inoculum and only appears in infected cells.
claims.source: The HDV antigenome is a circular replication intermediate that is complementary to the genome. It is not present in the inoculum and only appears in infected cells (Chen et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 1986.

claims.claim: NTCP is functionally conserved in mammalians, but protein sequences of NTCP vary among species, which is likely to contribute to the narrow species tropism of viral infection.
claims.source: NTCP is functionally conserved in mammalians, but protein sequences of NTCP vary among species, which is likely to contribute to the narrow species tropism of viral infection.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of sequence variation and functional differences among species.

claims.claim: The interaction between NTCP and L protein of HBV is highly specific.
claims.source: Whereas HBV first attaches to hepatocytes mainly through heparan sulfate (Schulze et al., 2007; Leistner et al., 2008), our data demonstrate that the interaction between NTCP and L protein of HBV is highly specific, and NTCP is crucial for productive viral entry of hepatocytes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: NTCP is crucial for productive viral entry of hepatocytes.
claims.source: Whereas HBV first attaches to hepatocytes mainly through heparan sulfate (Schulze et al., 2007; Leistner et al., 2008), our data demonstrate that the interaction between NTCP and L protein of HBV is highly specific, and NTCP is crucial for productive viral entry of hepatocytes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: The newly discovered role of NTCP as an entry receptor for HBV and HDV raises interesting questions regarding its involvement in viral pathogenesis.
claims.source: The newly discovered role of NTCP as an entry receptor for HBV and HDV raises interesting questions regarding its involvement in viral pathogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claims.claim: Identification of NTCP as a functional receptor for HBV and HDV advances our understanding of their entry into host cells and may lead to new prevention and treatment strategies against these viruses and related diseases.
claims.source: Identification of NTCP as a functional receptor for HBV and HDV advances our understanding of their entry into host cells and may lead to new prevention and treatment strategies against these viruses and related diseases.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the findings.

results.result: HBV and HDV infections represent a major global health burden. Approximately 2 billion people have been infected with HBV worldwide, with over 350 million chronically infected. HBV-related diseases cause approximately 1 million deaths per year, and coinfection with HDV increases disease severity.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide epidemiological context from established literature, supported by appropriate citations. These are well-established facts about HBV/HDV disease burden and serve as background knowledge for the study.

results.result: The pre-S1 domain of the HBV L envelope protein is critical for viral entry and believed to mediate receptor binding, but no functional receptor had been confirmed prior to this study. HDV, which carries HBV envelope proteins, has similar entry mechanisms and serves as a surrogate for studying HBV entry.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C12 establish the biological background and rationale for the study, supported by multiple citations to prior literature. These claims accurately represent the state of knowledge before this work and justify the research question.

results.result: A photoreactive peptide ligand (WTb) derived from the pre-S1 domain retains biological activity and specifically inhibits HBV and HDV infection. The F14L mutation does not affect HDV binding, while the N9K mutation (N9Kb peptide) abolishes inhibitory activity, providing an appropriate negative control.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C16 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1B-D showing that WTb inhibits viral binding and infection comparably to the native peptide, while N9Kb does not. This validates the probe design for subsequent receptor identification experiments.

results.result: Photo-cross-linking with WTb identifies a specific ~65 kDa glycoprotein in primary Tupaia and human hepatocytes. The protein is highly N-glycosylated (shifts to ~43 kDa upon deglycosylation), contains no intermolecular disulfide bonds, and shows specific competition with native pre-S1 peptide but not the N9K mutant.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C22 are supported by Western blot data in Figure 2A-D showing specific cross-linking, glycosylation sensitivity, and competitive binding. The specificity is demonstrated by the lack of cross-linking with N9Kb and competition experiments. The decrease in abundance over time in culture (C21) is consistent with known hepatocyte behavior.

results.result: Mass spectrometry analysis of the cross-linked protein identified Tupaia NTCP, which shares 83.9% sequence identity with human NTCP and has a 30 amino acid insertion near its C-terminus.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 are supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 2—figure supplement 5) identifying two tryptic peptides matching NTCP, including one containing the Tupaia-specific insertion. The sequence analysis in Figure 2F confirms the identity and structural features.

results.result: Recombinant human and Tupaia NTCP expressed in heterologous cells specifically bind the WTb peptide and native pre-S1 peptides, and support HDV virion binding. The N9K mutation in either the peptide or viral L protein abolishes binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C29 are supported by multiple complementary experiments in Figure 3A-D: cross-linking of recombinant NTCP, co-localization with fluorescent peptides, FACS analysis, and HDV binding assays. The specificity is demonstrated by the consistent loss of binding with N9K mutations.

results.result: siRNA-mediated knockdown of NTCP in primary Tupaia hepatocytes significantly reduces HDV and HBV infection as measured by viral RNA and antigen levels. NTCP knockdown does not affect control viruses (Lenti-VSV-G, AAV8-HBV) that use different entry mechanisms, demonstrating specificity for the viral entry step.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C34 are supported by comprehensive data in Figure 4A showing that NTCP knockdown reduces both HDV genomic and antigenomic RNA (indicating de novo infection), HBV antigens, and viral RNAs, while not affecting control viruses. The specificity controls (C32, C34) are critical and well-executed.

results.result: NTCP expression increases dramatically upon differentiation of HepaRG cells, and knockdown of hNTCP in differentiated HepaRG cells reduces both HDV and HBV infection as measured by viral RNA and antigen levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 are supported by data in Figure 4B showing correlation between NTCP expression and susceptibility to infection, and significant reduction in viral markers upon NTCP knockdown. This validates the findings in a human cell system.

results.result: Knockdown of hNTCP in primary human hepatocytes significantly reduces HBV infection in a manner correlated with knockdown efficiency, as measured by viral antigens and RNAs.
results.evaluation: Claim C38 is supported by data in Figure 4C showing dose-dependent reduction in HBV infection markers correlating with NTCP knockdown efficiency in PHHs, the natural target cells for HBV. This is critical validation in the most physiologically relevant system.

results.result: Exogenous expression of hNTCP renders non-susceptible Huh-7 cells susceptible to HDV infection with efficiency comparable to primary hepatocytes. The infection is genuine (produces replicating antigenomic RNA), can be blocked by known entry inhibitors, and correlates with both viral dose and NTCP expression level.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 are supported by comprehensive data in Figure 5 showing that NTCP expression is necessary and sufficient for HDV infection. The demonstration of antigenomic RNA production (C43) is critical evidence for genuine infection rather than just binding. The dose-response relationships (C44) and inhibitor sensitivity (C42) provide strong validation.

results.result: Exogenous expression of NTCP renders HepG2 cells susceptible to HBV infection, producing all expected viral replication intermediates including cccDNA, viral RNAs, and antigens. The infection is dose-dependent, can be blocked by entry inhibitors, and shows kinetics consistent with de novo infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C51 are supported by extensive data in Figure 6 and supplements showing HBV infection markers including the critical cccDNA intermediate (C49-C50), which is the definitive marker of authentic HBV infection. The kinetic analysis (C50-C51) and inhibitor sensitivity (C47, C50) provide strong evidence for genuine infection at the entry level.

results.result: HBV infection efficiency in HepG2-NTCP cells is comparable to that in primary human hepatocytes when measured by intracellular staining, though HBeAg secretion levels differ while viral RNA levels per cell are similar.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 are supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplements 2-3 comparing infection efficiency between HepG2-NTCP and PHHs. The comparison is appropriate and shows that NTCP expression confers physiologically relevant susceptibility.

results.result: Both HepG2-NTCP cells and primary human hepatocytes produce low levels of progeny viral DNA in culture medium despite significant HBeAg secretion and intracellular viral replication, resulting in limited secondary infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 are supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplements 4-5 and citations. This is an important observation about the limitations of the in vitro system and is appropriately discussed as potentially due to missing host factors or inhibitory factors in culture.

results.result: Despite 96.3% sequence identity between human and monkey NTCP, monkey NTCP does not support viral infection. Amino acids 157-165 of NTCP are critical for pre-S1 binding and viral infection: replacing these residues in hNTCP with monkey residues abolishes function, while the reciprocal substitution in mkNTCP restores function for both HDV and HBV.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C57 are supported by comprehensive mutagenesis data in Figure 7 showing that a small motif (9 amino acids) determines species specificity. The reciprocal swap experiments provide strong evidence for the functional importance of this region. This is elegant structure-function analysis.

results.result: NTCP is a functional receptor for both HBV and HDV, with highly specific interaction with the L protein that is crucial for productive viral entry of hepatocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C58, C82, C83 represent the main conclusion, which is strongly supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence: biochemical identification, binding studies, loss-of-function (knockdown), gain-of-function (complementation), and structure-function analysis. The evidence is comprehensive and compelling.

results.result: NTCP is a liver-specific, basolateral membrane bile acid transporter with properties consistent with its role as an HBV/HDV receptor. Its tissue distribution, subcellular localization, and membrane topology are appropriate for a receptor for blood-borne hepatotropic viruses.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C65 provide important biological context about NTCP, supported by appropriate citations. These established properties of NTCP make biological sense for a viral receptor and strengthen the plausibility of the findings.

results.result: NTCP expression decreases rapidly in cultured primary hepatocytes and is inversely correlated with hepatocyte dedifferentiation in cancer and liver disease severity. This may explain the limited window of susceptibility of primary hepatocytes to HBV infection in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by citations and the authors' own data (Figure 2C). This provides important context for understanding the biology of HBV infection and the challenges of in vitro infection systems.

results.result: Tupaia (treeshrews) are the only species other than humans and chimpanzees susceptible to HBV infection. HepaRG is the only cell line susceptible to HBV/HDV upon differentiation, which requires a lengthy culture procedure.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 provide methodological context supported by appropriate citations. These facts justify the choice of experimental systems used in the study.

results.result: HDV can only infect cells in a single round in the absence of HBV, and the antigenomic RNA is a replication intermediate that only appears in infected cells, making it a definitive marker of de novo infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 are supported by citations and represent established knowledge about HDV biology. This justifies the use of HDV as a surrogate for studying HBV entry and the use of antigenomic RNA as a marker of genuine infection.

results.result: NTCP is functionally conserved in mammals but shows sequence variation among species, which likely contributes to the narrow species tropism of HBV/HDV infection.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 is supported by the mutagenesis data showing that small sequence differences determine species specificity (C52-C57). This is a reasonable inference from the experimental data.

results.result: The identification of NTCP as an HBV/HDV receptor raises questions about its role in viral pathogenesis and may lead to new prevention and treatment strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 are speculative statements about future implications. While reasonable, they are not directly supported by data in this manuscript and represent potential future directions rather than demonstrated results.
